key_insight: KMed-31B combines task-specialist training with multi-teacher distillation to improve medical dialogue benchmark scores while maintaining or slightly improving multiple-choice medical performance.
clinical_relevance: The approach could support institutions developing on-premises medical language models, but benchmark gains do not establish clinical safety or patient benefit.
method: Divide medical tasks into four categories by expected output and available feedback, then train a specialist for each.
Build Synthetic Health Dialogue from simulated consultations covering common primary-care presentations.
Integrate specialists into one student using Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD²).
evidence_signal: In thinking mode, HealthBench Hard rose from 23.80 to 51.48 and Professional from 41.97 to 59.18; four multiple-choice benchmark scores were maintained or slightly improved, and the recipe also improved another base model.
watch_item: The abstract reports benchmark evaluations rather than prospective clinical deployment; real-world safety and local hardware requirements need validation.
